title: How your phone finds you from 20,000 km up
description:
Your phone never transmits to GPS satellites: each one broadcasts where it is and exactly when it sent the signal. Travel time times the speed of light gives a distance (about 67 thousandths of a second from 20,200 km), so you're on a sphere around each satellite; three spheres meet in two points, and one is out in space. But a phone's clock off by a millionth of a second puts every distance 300 m out, so a fourth satellite gives four equations for four unknowns: your three coordinates and your clock's error. And the satellites' clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day from relativity, which would add up to about 11 km of error a day if it weren't corrected.

Numbers checked in code (signal times, clock error in metres, and 2,000 simulated position fixes with 4 satellites and a clock 1 microsecond off). Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Positioning_System https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_analysis_for_the_Global_Positioning_System

social_caption: Your phone never talks to GPS satellites. Here's how four clocks in space and one cheap clock in your pocket find you to within 5 meters.
facts_checked: GPS satellites orbit about 20,200 km up (20,180-20,184 km); signal from overhead takes 67 ms at light speed (verify.py; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Positioning_System)

Receivers are passive: satellites broadcast their position and send time; at least 4 satellites are needed for x, y, z and the receiver clock offset (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Positioning_System)
1 microsecond of clock error x speed of light = 300 m (verify.py)

4 satellites with a phone clock 1 us off: position recovered to millimetres and the 1 us clock error solved (2,000 simulated fixes, verify.py); 3 satellites with the clock error ignored: hundreds of metres off
Smartphones accurate to 4.9 m or better (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Positioning_System)
Satellite clocks gain 38.6 us/day (+45.8 gravity, -7.2 speed); uncorrected ~11.4 km/day of position error (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_analysis_for_the_Global_Positioning_System)
With height known (at sea), 3 unknowns remain (2 position + clock): 3 satellites (verify.py reasoning)

beats.say: How does your phone find you from space?
It never sends anything up. The satellites don't even know you exist. They just shout the time.
Each one, 20,000 kilometers up, keeps saying: here's where I am, and here's exactly when I sent this.
beats.caption: Each one, 20,000 km up, keeps saying: here's where I am, and here's exactly when I sent this.

beats.say: Hear one. Its signal took 67 thousandths of a second. Times the speed of light, you're 20,000 kilometers away. Somewhere on a giant sphere.
beats.caption: Hear one. Its signal took 0.067 seconds. Times the speed of light, you're 20,000 km away. Somewhere on a giant sphere.

beats.say: Hear a second. Two spheres cross in a circle.
A third cuts that circle at two points. One is out in space. The other is you.
But your phone's clock is cheap. Off by one millionth of a second, and every distance is 300 meters wrong.
beats.caption: But your phone's clock is cheap. Off by a millionth of a second, and every distance is 300 m wrong.

beats.say: So listen to a fourth. Now there are four unknowns: three for where you are, one for how wrong your clock is. Four signals solve all four.
Your cheap phone just borrowed four atomic clocks. That's how it finds you to about 5 meters.
beats.caption: Your cheap phone just borrowed four atomic clocks. That's how it finds you to about 5 m.

beats.say: One more catch. Up there, time runs fast: 38 millionths of a second a day. Left alone, that's 11 kilometers off by tomorrow.
beats.caption: One more catch. Up there, time runs fast: 38 µs a day. Left alone, that's 11 km off by tomorrow.

beats.say: So your phone never knows where it is. It knows when, and works out where.
On a ship, where your height is known, how many satellites do you need?
